strengths: Clear and simple idea: transferring RMT-style memory tokens and segment-level recurrent training to the Decision Transformer setting, with a reasonably detailed description of the training procedure (Figures 2-4).
Includes several ablations (number of segments, memory size, presence of memory tokens via DT-XL, segment overlap/memory fixation) that help interpret the design choices.
Attention-map analysis of read/write memory tokens gives some qualitative insight into how the memory tokens are attended to.
Code and weights are stated to be publicly released; hyperparameters are listed.
weaknesses: Central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. On Atari, all gains over DT-XL are within one standard deviation with only 3 seeds x 10 episodes and no statistical tests, yet the paper calls them 'significant'. On MuJoCo, the mean (75.2) is essentially equal to DT (74.7) and below CQL (77.6), while the conclusion claims RMDT 'significantly outperforms' DT, Transformer-XL, and TAP.

The best MuJoCo configuration uses 'memory fixation' after the first segment, which seems to disable the recurrent memory update that is the paper's core contribution; the variant with genuinely recurrent memory (RMDT-dagger) collapses to a mean of 45.0. This raises serious doubts about whether the recurrent memory mechanism actually works in continuous control.

No evaluation on tasks that actually require long-term memory (e.g., POMDP or memory benchmarks). Atari with frame stacking and MuJoCo locomotion are largely Markovian, so the experiments cannot demonstrate the claimed benefit of long-context memory; attention maps do not establish causal use of memory content.

Limited novelty: a direct combination of RMT and DT with no new mechanism; the paper does not compare to other memory-augmented or long-context sequence-model RL baselines, and DT-XL is not evaluated on MuJoCo. DT baseline numbers on MuJoCo are copied from another paper rather than re-run under identical conditions.

Very high variance in MuJoCo results (e.g., +/-14.4, +/-18.9, +/-16.1) and only four Atari games, making the evaluation unconvincing; the claim that context scaling without memory doesn't help is asserted but not shown with a direct DT context-90/150 comparison.

Presentation issues: duplicate references [8] and [9], typos ('MoJoko', 'Transformative models'), duplicated Figure 10 caption, unclear definition of DT-XL and of 'memory fixation', and confusing description of the segment/overlap procedure.
